triage.name: Bad Breath
triage.reason: Common complaint with a focused differential (oral hygiene, gingival disease, sinus or GI causes); diagnosis largely by history and exam, though the presentation is less classic for a full case.

demographics: Adults are affected more often than children
Prevalence rises with age as gum disease and dry mouth become more common
More often reported by people who smoke or use tobacco

risk_factors.text: Poor oral hygiene (infrequent brushing or flossing)
Dry mouth from medicines or mouth breathing
Dental cavities, ill-fitting dentures or oral infections
Recent intake of strong-smelling foods such as raw onion, garlic or cabbage
Postnasal drip, sinusitis or chronic nasal problems

social_history: Irregular dental care or long interval since last dental visit

chief_complaints.text: People step back when I talk to them
I have a bad taste in my mouth

hpi.onset: Gradual, often noticed by the patient or pointed out by family, friends or coworkers
hpi.duration: Usually weeks to months; may be long-standing
hpi.progression: Persistent or slowly worsening; often worse in the morning and between meals
hpi.location: Mouth and breath; sometimes described as coming from the nose or stomach
hpi.quality: Foul, stale or sulfur-like odor; may be described as a bad taste
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; bothersome socially rather than physically painful
hpi.timing: Worse on waking, when hungry, after strong-smelling meals, and when the mouth is dry
aggravating: Eating raw onion, garlic or cabbage

associated_symptoms.text: Bleeding or tender gums when brushing
Heartburn or sour taste after meals

pertinent_negatives: Blood in stool or black stools
Loose teeth or new gum recession

argues_against: Severe unilateral facial pain with fever (sinusitis or dental abscess)
Loose teeth or purulent gum discharge

positives.text: Heartburn or sour taste after meals

argues_against: Advanced kidney or liver disease (ammonia-like or musty breath)

atypical.how_it_differs: Often noticed by a parent rather than the child; may be linked to a foreign body in the nose, thumb sucking or poor brushing habits.
More often due to dry mouth from medicines, dentures, gum disease or reduced saliva flow; may be less aware of the odor.
May be worsened by pregnancy gingivitis, dry mouth, reflux or morning sickness; usually improves after delivery with good dental care.
Can have a fruity or acetone-like odor when blood sugars are very high, or a dry mouth from high glucose; needs evaluation for ketoacidosis if severe.
Breath may smell like ammonia or urine when kidney function is advanced; oral causes are still common and should be checked first.
Breath may have a musty or sweet odor with advanced liver disease; oral hygiene and dental disease remain common contributors.

general.mild: Well-appearing, comfortable, no distress; normal speech and interaction
general.moderate: Well-appearing but may seem self-conscious or avoid close conversation; no systemic signs
general.severe: Well-appearing, no acute distress; odor is prominent and noticeable from a distance
general.critical: Not applicable; bad breath itself is not a critical illness, but a toxic-appearing patient suggests a serious underlying cause such as a deep dental or sinus infection or systemic disease

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to exhale slowly through the mouth while you stand close, or have them speak and assess the odor
findings.finding: Foul, stale or sulfur-like breath odor

findings.maneuver: Inspect the dorsum of the tongue, especially the posterior third
findings.finding: White or yellowish coating on the tongue surface

findings.maneuver: Inspect the gums for redness, swelling, and bleeding, and gently probe the gingival margins
findings.finding: Red, swollen or bleeding gums suggesting gingivitis or periodontal disease

findings.maneuver: Inspect the teeth for visible decay, discoloration, or broken or missing teeth
findings.finding: Dental caries, plaque, or debris on the teeth

findings.maneuver: Inspect the mouth for plaque, food debris, and overall cleanliness
findings.finding: Visible plaque, food debris, or heavy bacterial buildup

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral mucosa and tongue for moisture; note pooling of saliva
findings.finding: Dry oral mucosa with reduced saliva, suggesting xerostomia

findings.maneuver: Inspect the posterior pharynx for mucus dripping down the back of the throat
findings.finding: Postnasal drip or mucopurulent discharge in the posterior pharynx

findings.maneuver: Inspect the nasal passages for congestion, discharge, or polyps
findings.finding: Nasal congestion or purulent nasal discharge suggesting sinusitis

findings.maneuver: Perform a complete oral examination including teeth, gums, tongue, and mucosa
findings.finding: No caries, no gingival disease, no tongue coating, and normal moisture

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the face and jaw for swelling or tenderness
findings.finding: No facial swelling, no jaw tenderness, no trismus
No enlarged or tender cervical lymph nodes

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen for tenderness, masses, or organomegaly
findings.finding: Soft, non-tender abdomen without masses or hepatosplenomegaly
Clear breath sounds without crackles or wheezing

labs.caveat: Only relevant when a fruity or acetone-like odor suggests hyperglycemia or ketoacidosis; a normal glucose makes a metabolic cause unlikely.
Screens for undiagnosed diabetes when dry mouth or recurrent oral infection is a factor.
Only when an ammonia-like or urine-like breath odor suggests advanced kidney disease.
Rises with advanced kidney disease; supports a uremic cause of the odor.
Only when a musty or sweet odor suggests advanced liver disease.
Only useful when a deep dental, periodontal or sinus infection is suspected; halitosis itself does not raise the white count.

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected dental caries, periodontal disease or dental abscess

findings.text: Alveolar bone loss from periodontal disease
Impacted or partially erupted tooth with surrounding debris

imaging.preferred_when: Chronic or recurrent sinus symptoms with purulent postnasal drip

findings.text: Mucosal thickening or opacification of one or more sinuses

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected deep neck or dental space infection

findings.text: Dental root abscess with surrounding soft tissue inflammation
Deep neck space fluid collection or abscess

imaging.preferred_when: Reflux or gastric symptoms that persist despite treatment

initial.why: Looks for leukocytosis if a deep dental, periodontal or sinus infection is suspected
initial.only_if: fever, facial pain or swelling, or purulent discharge suggests infection

initial.why: Checks for hyperglycemia when a fruity or acetone-like odor or dry mouth is present
initial.only_if: fruity breath odor, excessive thirst or frequent urination

initial.why: Screens for undiagnosed diabetes contributing to dry mouth or recurrent oral infection
initial.only_if: risk factors for diabetes or recurrent oral infections

initial.why: Identifies caries, periodontal bone loss or dental abscess not visible on exam
initial.only_if: dental disease is suspected on oral examination

supporting.why: Assesses kidney function when an ammonia-like or urine-like odor suggests uremia
supporting.only_if: ammonia-like breath odor or known kidney disease

supporting.why: Supports a uremic cause when kidney function is reduced
supporting.only_if: ammonia-like breath odor or known kidney disease

supporting.why: Evaluates for liver disease when a musty or sweet odor is present
supporting.only_if: musty or sweet breath odor or signs of liver disease

supporting.why: Screens for hepatic dysfunction as a cause of the odor
supporting.only_if: musty or sweet breath odor or signs of liver disease

supporting.why: Screens for hepatic dysfunction as a cause of the odor
supporting.only_if: musty or sweet breath odor or signs of liver disease

supporting.why: Confirms chronic sinusitis when nasal symptoms and postnasal drip dominate
supporting.only_if: chronic or recurrent sinus symptoms persist

supporting.why: Defines the extent of a suspected deep dental or neck space infection
supporting.only_if: severe facial pain, swelling, trismus or toxic appearance

supporting.why: Evaluates reflux or gastric disease when GI symptoms persist despite treatment

Not routine unless a metabolic odor or diabetes symptoms are present
Not routine for isolated bad breath
Not routine unless uremic odor or kidney disease is suspected
Not routine unless uremic odor or kidney disease is suspected
Not routine unless liver disease is suspected

Not routine unless liver disease is suspected

Not needed when the oral examination is completely normal

decision_points: Bad breath is diagnosed clinically from history and examination; routine laboratory testing is not required.
If the oral examination is normal, evaluate the nose, sinuses and pharynx before considering systemic causes.
A fruity or acetone-like odor with hyperglycemia should prompt evaluation for diabetic ketoacidosis.
An ammonia-like or urine-like odor should prompt assessment of kidney function.
A musty or sweet odor with jaundice or other liver signs should prompt assessment of liver function.
Fever, facial swelling, trismus or a toxic appearance suggests a deep dental or sinus infection and needs urgent imaging and treatment.

differential.name: Gingivitis and periodontal disease
differential.why_considered: The most common cause of halitosis; bacteria in plaque and periodontal pockets produce volatile sulfur compounds.

history: Long interval since last dental visit
exam: Red, swollen or bleeding gingival margins
Heavy plaque or calculus on the teeth
imaging: Alveolar bone loss on panoramic dental radiograph

differential.name: Dental caries or dental abscess
differential.why_considered: Decayed or infected teeth harbor bacteria and debris that cause foul odor and bad taste.
differential.trigger: Fever, facial swelling, trismus or severe localized tooth pain

exam: Visible decay, broken tooth or discoloration
Trismus or tenderness over the affected tooth
labs: Leukocytosis if a deep infection is present
imaging: Periapical lucency or dental caries on panoramic radiograph
Dental root abscess with soft tissue inflammation on CT neck

differential.name: Chronic sinusitis or postnasal drip
differential.why_considered: Mucopurulent nasal discharge dripping into the pharynx can cause bad breath and a bad taste.

exam: Mucopurulent drip in the posterior pharynx
imaging: Mucosal thickening or opacification of sinuses on CT

differential.name: Xerostomia (dry mouth)
differential.why_considered: Reduced saliva flow allows bacteria and debris to accumulate, worsening breath odor.

history: Use of anticholinergic, antihistamine or antidepressant medicines
exam: Dry oral mucosa with reduced saliva
Little or no pooling of saliva on the floor of the mouth

differential.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
differential.why_considered: Reflux of gastric contents can cause a sour taste and contribute to bad breath.

history: Heartburn or sour taste after meals
imaging: Esophagitis or hiatal hernia on upper endoscopy if symptoms persist

differential.name: Diabetic ketoacidosis
differential.why_considered: A fruity or acetone-like breath odor can be mistaken for ordinary halitosis but signals a metabolic emergency.
differential.trigger: Fruity or acetone-like breath odor with excessive thirst, frequent urination or hyperglycemia

exam: Altered mental status in severe cases

differential.name: Advanced kidney disease (uremia)
differential.why_considered: An ammonia-like or urine-like breath odor can occur with advanced renal failure.
differential.trigger: Ammonia-like or urine-like breath odor with known or suspected kidney disease

exam: Dry or uremic frost on the skin in severe cases

differential.name: Advanced liver disease
differential.why_considered: A musty or sweet breath odor can occur with advanced hepatic dysfunction.
differential.trigger: Musty or sweet breath odor with jaundice or other signs of liver disease

history: Known liver disease or heavy alcohol use

severity.mild: Occasional bad breath noticed mainly on waking or after strong-smelling foods; responds to brushing, flossing and fluids; no oral disease on examination.
severity.moderate: Persistent daily bad breath with visible plaque, tongue coating, gingival inflammation or dry mouth; socially bothersome but no systemic signs.
severity.severe: Prominent odor noticeable from a distance, often with significant periodontal disease, dental decay or chronic sinusitis; may affect quality of life and social interaction.
severity.critical: Not applicable to halitosis itself; a toxic-appearing patient with fever, facial swelling or trismus suggests a deep dental or sinus infection or a systemic metabolic cause and requires urgent evaluation.

red_flags.finding: Fever with facial swelling, trismus or severe localized tooth pain
red_flags.meaning: Deep dental or neck space infection; needs urgent imaging and treatment

red_flags.finding: Fruity or acetone-like breath odor with excessive thirst or frequent urination
red_flags.meaning: Possible diabetic ketoacidosis; check glucose and ketones urgently
Possible advanced kidney disease; assess renal function

red_flags.finding: Musty or sweet breath odor with jaundice or confusion
red_flags.meaning: Possible advanced liver disease or hepatic encephalopathy; assess liver function

red_flags.finding: Difficulty swallowing, drooling or voice change
red_flags.meaning: Possible deep neck infection or airway compromise; urgent evaluation needed

complications.name: Progression of periodontal disease with tooth loss
Spread of dental infection to deep neck spaces

special_populations.differences: Often noticed by a parent rather than the child; consider a foreign body in the nose, thumb sucking or poor brushing habits. Dental caries and gingivitis are common contributors.
More often due to dry mouth from medicines, dentures, gum disease or reduced saliva flow; may be less aware of the odor.
May be worsened by pregnancy gingivitis, dry mouth, reflux or morning sickness; usually improves after delivery with good dental care.
Can have a fruity or acetone-like odor when blood sugars are very high, or a dry mouth from high glucose; needs evaluation for ketoacidosis if severe.
Breath may smell like ammonia or urine when kidney function is advanced; oral causes are still common and should be checked first.
Breath may have a musty or sweet odor with advanced liver disease; oral hygiene and dental disease remain common contributors.

key_questions.question: When did you first notice the bad breath, and is it there all the time or only at certain times?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks to months; worse on waking, when hungry, after strong-smelling meals, and when the mouth is dry

key_questions.question: How often do you brush and floss, and when was your last dental visit?
key_questions.looking_for: Infrequent brushing or flossing and a long interval since the last dental visit point to an oral cause

key_questions.question: Do your gums bleed or feel tender when you brush?
key_questions.looking_for: Bleeding or tender gums suggesting gingivitis or periodontal disease

key_questions.question: Does your mouth feel dry, or do you breathe through your mouth?
key_questions.looking_for: Dry mouth or mouth breathing, which allows bacteria and debris to accumulate

key_questions.question: Do you have a bad taste in your mouth, or a coating on your tongue?
key_questions.looking_for: Bad taste and tongue coating, which support an oral source

key_questions.question: Have you eaten raw onion, garlic or cabbage recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent intake of strong-smelling foods as a dietary cause

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or use chewing tobacco?
key_questions.looking_for: Tobacco use, which causes its own odor and worsens gum disease and dry mouth

key_questions.question: Do you have nasal congestion, postnasal drip or facial pressure?
key_questions.looking_for: Nasal or sinus symptoms suggesting postnasal drip or chronic sinusitis

key_questions.question: Do you have heartburn or a sour taste after meals?
key_questions.looking_for: Reflux symptoms that may contribute to the odor

key_questions.question: What medicines do you take, including anything for allergies, mood or blood pressure?
key_questions.looking_for: Anticholinergics, antihistamines, diuretics, antidepressants or metformin that can cause dry mouth

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever, facial swelling, trouble swallowing or loose teeth?
key_questions.looking_for: Signs of a deep dental or sinus infection or airway compromise that need urgent evaluation

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, kidney disease or liver disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions that can produce a fruity, ammonia-like or musty breath odor

key_questions.question: Have you had any weight loss, excessive thirst or frequent urination?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms suggesting an underlying metabolic cause such as hyperglycemia

reasoning_points: Bad breath is diagnosed clinically from the history and a focused oral, nasal and pharyngeal examination; routine laboratory testing is not required.
The most common causes are oral: poor oral hygiene, gingivitis or periodontal disease, dental caries, tongue coating and dry mouth.
Nasal and sinus disease with postnasal drip is the next most common source when the oral examination is normal.
Dietary intake of strong-smelling foods such as raw onion, garlic or cabbage and tobacco use are common contributors.
A fruity or acetone-like odor suggests hyperglycemia or ketoacidosis; an ammonia-like or urine-like odor suggests advanced kidney disease; a musty or sweet odor suggests advanced liver disease.
Fever, facial swelling, trismus or a toxic appearance suggests a deep dental or sinus infection and needs urgent imaging and treatment.
Social and psychological distress is a common consequence even when the odor is mild.

easy: Adult with obvious poor oral hygiene, visible plaque and gingival inflammation
Bad breath worse on waking and after strong-smelling meals
Symptoms improve with brushing, flossing and mouthwash
No systemic symptoms and a normal general examination
medium: Normal oral examination but chronic nasal congestion and postnasal drip suggesting sinusitis
Dry mouth from anticholinergic or antihistamine medicines
Reflux symptoms with a sour taste after meals
Long-standing bad breath with significant periodontal disease and gum recession
hard: Fruity or acetone-like breath odor in a patient with undiagnosed diabetes
Ammonia-like or urine-like breath odor in a patient with advanced kidney disease
Musty or sweet breath odor with jaundice or confusion suggesting advanced liver disease
Child with a foreign body in the nose and unilateral foul nasal discharge
Older adult with dentures and reduced saliva flow who is unaware of the odor
